{{Short description|Angle between the two sightlines or two objects as viewed from an observer}}
{{no footnotes|date=September 2025}}
'''Angular distance''' or '''angular separation''' is the measure of the [[angle]] between the [[orientation (geometry)|orientation]] of two [[straight line]]s, [[ray (geometry)|ray]]s, or [[vector (geometry)|vector]]s – typically in [[three-dimensional space]] – or the [[central angle]] [[subtended]] by the [[radius|radii]] through two points on a [[sphere]]. When the rays are [[Line of sight|lines of sight]] from an observer to two points in space, it is known as the '''apparent distance''' or '''apparent separation'''.

Angular distance appears in [[mathematics]] (in particular [[geometry]] and [[trigonometry]]) and all [[natural science]]s (e.g., [[kinematics]], [[astronomy]], and [[geophysics]]). In the [[classical mechanics]] of rotating objects, it appears alongside [[angular velocity]], [[angular acceleration]], [[angular momentum]], [[moment of inertia]] and [[torque]].

==Measurement==
As an angle, the angular separation is measured using [[angular unit]]s such as [[Degree (angle)|degrees]] or [[radian]]s, using instruments such as [[goniometer]]s or optical instruments specially designed to point in well-defined directions and record the corresponding angles (such as [[telescope]]s).

== Celestial coordinates ==
[[File:Fig angle separation.png|thumb|Angular separation <math>\theta</math> between points A and B as seen from O]]
To derive the equation that describes the angular separation of two points located on the surface of a sphere as seen from the center of the sphere, we use the example of two [[astronomical objects]] <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> observed from the Earth. The objects <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are defined by their [[celestial coordinate system| celestial coordinates]], namely their [[Right ascension|right ascensions (RA)]], <math>(\alpha_A, \alpha_B)\in [0, 2\pi]</math>; and [[Declination|declinations (dec)]], <math>(\delta_A, \delta_B) \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]</math>. Let <math>O</math> indicate the observer on Earth, assumed to be located at the center of the [[celestial sphere]]. The [[dot product]] of the vectors <math>\mathbf{OA}</math> and <math>\mathbf{OB}</math> is equal to:
:<math>\mathbf{OA}\cdot\mathbf{OB}= R^2 \cos\theta</math> 
which is equivalent to:
:<math>\mathbf{n_A} \cdot \mathbf{n_B} = \cos\theta</math>

In the <math>(x,y,z)</math> frame, the two unitary vectors are decomposed into:
<math display="block">\mathbf{n_A} = 
\begin{pmatrix}
 \cos\delta_A \cos\alpha_A\\
 \cos\delta_A \sin\alpha_A\\
  \sin\delta_A
\end{pmatrix} 
\mathrm{\qquad  and \qquad }
\mathbf{n_B} = 
\begin{pmatrix}
 \cos\delta_B \cos\alpha_B\\
 \cos\delta_B \sin\alpha_B\\
  \sin\delta_B
\end{pmatrix} .
</math>
Therefore, 
<math display="block">\mathbf{n_A} \cdot \mathbf{n_B} = \cos\delta_A \cos\alpha_A \cos\delta_B \cos\alpha_B + \cos\delta_A \sin\alpha_A \cos\delta_B \sin\alpha_B + \sin\delta_A \sin\delta_B \equiv \cos\theta</math>
then:
:<math>\theta = \cos^{-1}\left[\sin\delta_A \sin\delta_B + \cos\delta_A \cos\delta_B \cos(\alpha_A - \alpha_B)\right]</math>

=== Small angular distance approximation ===
The above expression is valid for any position of A and B on the sphere. In astronomy, it often happens that the considered objects are really close in the sky: stars in a telescope field of view, binary stars, the satellites of the giant planets of the [[Solar System]], etc. In the case where <math>\theta\ll 1</math> radian, implying <math>\alpha_A-\alpha_B\ll 1</math> and <math>\delta_A-\delta_B\ll 1</math>, we can develop the above expression and simplify it. In the [[small-angle approximation]], at second order, the above expression becomes:
:<math>\cos\theta \approx 1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2} \approx \sin\delta_A \sin\delta_B + \cos\delta_A \cos\delta_B \left[1 - \frac{(\alpha_A - \alpha_B)^2}{2}\right]</math>
meaning
:<math>1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2} \approx \cos(\delta_A-\delta_B) - \cos\delta_A\cos\delta_B \frac{(\alpha_A - \alpha_B)^2}{2}</math>
hence
:<math>1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2} \approx 1 - \frac{(\delta_A-\delta_B)^2}{2} - \cos\delta_A\cos\delta_B \frac{(\alpha_A - \alpha_B)^2}{2}</math>.
Given that <math>\delta_A-\delta_B\ll 1</math> and <math>\alpha_A-\alpha_B\ll 1</math>, at a second-order development it turns that <math>\cos\delta_A\cos\delta_B \frac{(\alpha_A - \alpha_B)^2}{2} \approx \cos^2\delta_A \frac{(\alpha_A - \alpha_B)^2}{2}</math>, so that
:<math>\theta \approx \sqrt{\left[(\alpha_A - \alpha_B)\cos\delta_A\right]^2 + (\delta_A-\delta_B)^2}</math>

=== Small angular distance: planar approximation ===
[[File:Fig angle separation planar.png|thumb|Planar approximation of angular distance on sky]]
If we consider a detector imaging a small sky field (dimension much less than one radian) with the <math>y</math>-axis pointing up, parallel to the meridian of right ascension <math>\alpha</math>, and the <math>x</math>-axis along the parallel of declination <math>\delta</math>, the angular separation can be written as:
: <math>\theta \approx \sqrt{\delta x^2 + \delta y^2}</math>
where <math>\delta x = (\alpha_A - \alpha_B)\cos\delta_A </math> and <math>\delta y=\delta_A-\delta_B</math>.

Note that the <math>y</math>-axis is equal to the declination, whereas the <math>x</math>-axis is the right ascension modulated by <math>\cos\delta_A</math> because the section of a sphere of radius <math>R</math> at declination (latitude) <math>\delta</math> is <math>R' = R \cos\delta_A</math> (see Figure).
